hints: Think about whether the $\text{-NO}_2$ group pushes electrons into the ring or pulls electrons away from the ring.
walkthrough:
Sort directors into two families**
Think of ring substituents as either electron donating, like $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-CH}_3$, which direct to 2,4,6 positions, or electron withdrawing, like $\text{-NO}_2$ and $\text{-CHO}$, which direct to 3,5 positions. The $\text{-NO}_2$ group has very electronegative N and O atoms pulling electron density away from the ring.

Link to the answer**
Because $\text{-NO}_2$ withdraws electrons it deactivates the 2,4,6 positions most strongly, so the next electrophile attacks at the meta 3 (and 5) position.
Final answer: $\text{-NO}_2$ is a meta directing group to positions 3 and 5, because it is a strongly electron withdrawing group.

hints: Remember that concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as an acid and $\text{HNO}_3$ acts as a base to generate the strong electrophile.
walkthrough:
See how the electrophile is made**
$\text{HNO}_3$ alone is not electrophilic enough to attack benzene. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ protonates $\text{HNO}_3$, which then loses water to leave the linear $\text{NO}_2^+$ nitronium ion.

Balance the equation**
One $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives one $\text{HSO}_4^-$ and one $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ alongside $\text{NO}_2^+$: $$\text{HNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NO}_2^+ + \text{HSO}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Look at compound Q and work backwards: it has two groups meta to each other, so which group must have been added first to direct meta?
walkthrough:
Read compound Q**
Q is 1,3 disubstituted: a $\text{COCH}_3$ group and a $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ isopropyl group meta to each other.

Decide the order**
Alkyl groups direct to 2,4 positions, acyl groups direct to 3,5 positions. To get a meta product, the meta director must go on first. So reaction 1 must be acylation to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$ as P, then alkylation in reaction 2 gives the meta isomer Q.
Final answer: Compound P is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3$, phenyl methyl ketone (acetophenone): benzene ring bonded to $\text{C(=O)CH}_3$.

hints: Recall which acyl chloride plus $\text{AlCl}_3$ installs a $\text{COCH}_3$ group, and which haloalkane installs a $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ group.
Match each catalyst to its halogen: chloride carrier $\text{AlCl}_3$ for acylation, bromide carrier $\text{FeBr}_3$ for bromoalkane alkylation.
walkthrough:
Install the acyl group first**
Reaction 1 is Friedel-Crafts acylation. Ethanoyl chloride provides the $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}^+$ electrophile with the Lewis acid catalyst anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + \text{HCl}$$

Install the alkyl group second**
Reaction 2 is Friedel-Crafts alkylation on deactivated P, directed meta by $\text{COCH}_3$. Use 2-bromopropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHBr}$, with $\text{FeBr}_3$ (or $\text{AlBr}_3$) to generate the $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^+$ type electrophile.

Final answer: reaction 1: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCl}$ + anhydrous $\text{AlCl}_3$
reaction 2: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHBr}$ + $\text{FeBr}_3$ (anhydrous, heat)

hints: Recall what a positive $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$ test looks like and what it tells you about breaking the $\text{C-Br}$ bond to release $\text{Br}^-$.
Compare the environment of Br: directly attached to the ring in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ versus attached to a $\text{CH}_2$ side chain in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$.
Think about how the lone pair on Br in bromobenzene can interact with the benzene $\pi$ system and what this does to $\text{C-Br}$ bond strength.
walkthrough:
Separate observation from explanation**
Warm $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$ detects free $\text{Br}^-$ as cream $\text{AgBr}$: $$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Br}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgBr}(s)$$ If the $\text{C-Br}$ bond hydrolyses, you see cream precipitate. If it does not break, you see no change.

Predict which bromide hydrolyses**
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ is a primary benzylic bromide. The $\text{C-Br}$ bond is a normal single bond and breaks readily on warming with water, releasing $\text{Br}^-$, so cream precipitate forms. $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ is an aryl bromide and does not hydrolyse under these conditions, so no precipitate.

Explain the aryl resistance**
In bromobenzene the Br atom has a p orbital lone pair that overlaps with the delocalised $\pi$ system of the ring. That delocalisation pulls electron density into the ring and gives the $\text{C-Br}$ bond partial double bond character. It is shorter and stronger, so hydrolysis does not occur.

Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ with $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$: no change, no precipitate.
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ with $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$: cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$.
Explanation: in $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ a lone pair on Br overlaps with the ring $\pi$ system, delocalised into the ring, giving the $\text{C-Br}$ bond partial double bond character so it is stronger and does not hydrolyse.

hints: Think of the two stages at the $\text{C=O}$ carbon: first water adds to make a tetrahedral intermediate, then $\text{Br}^-$ leaves.
walkthrough:
Name the two stage pattern**
Water as nucleophile first adds to the $\delta+$ carbonyl carbon to give a tetrahedral intermediate, then the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks to eliminate $\text{Br}^-$ and reform $\text{C=O}$. That is nucleophilic addition-elimination.
Final answer: (nucleophilic) addition-elimination

hints: Start by marking the polar $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ bond and the lone pairs on the O atom of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Think about where the curly arrow from the water lone pair goes and where the $\pi$ electrons of $\text{C=O}$ move to.
Draw the tetrahedral intermediate with correct charges: positive on the incoming $\text{OH}_2^+$ and negative on the original carbonyl O.
For the second step, decide which lone pair reforms the $\text{C=O}$ and which bond breaks to expel $\text{Br}^-$.
walkthrough:
Set up the addition attack**
You are beside the $\text{R-C(=O)-Br}$ molecule. Label the dipole $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$ because O is more electronegative. Show a lone pair on the O of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Draw a curly arrow from that lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$ atom, and a second curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ double bond up onto the O atom. Curly arrows always go from electron rich to electron poor.

Draw the tetrahedral intermediate**
The addition gives a tetrahedral carbon bonded to R, Br, OH and $\text{OH}_2^+$, with an $\text{O}^-$ (or OH after proton transfer) on the original carbonyl O. A common representation is $\text{RC(OH)(OH}_2^+)(\text{Br})(\text{O}^-)$ collapsing to $\text{RC(OH)}_2\text{Br}$. Check that charges balance and carbon has four single bonds.

Collapse by elimination**
Now reform the $\text{C=O}$. Take a lone pair on the $\text{O}^-$ and draw a curly arrow to form $\text{C=O}$. At the same time draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Br}$ sigma bond onto Br to expel $\text{Br}^-$. This is the elimination that restores the carbonyl and gives carboxylic acid plus $\text{HBr}$ after proton transfer.

Check examiner details**
Make sure every curly arrow starts at a lone pair or bond and ends at an atom or bond, all lone pairs involved are shown, dipoles $\delta+$ on C and $\delta-$ on O are shown, and charges on the intermediate and $\text{Br}^-$ are correct.

Final answer: Step 1 addition: lone pair on O of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, curly arrow $\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}^{\delta+}$ of $\text{C}^{\delta+}=\text{O}^{\delta-}$, curly arrow $\text{C=O} \rightarrow \text{O}$; intermediate $\text{RC(OH)(OH}_2^+)\text{Br}$ with $\text{O}^-$ protonated form, correctly drawn tetrahedral intermediate with charges.
Step 2 elimination: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ to reform $\text{C=O}$, curly arrow $\text{C-Br} \rightarrow \text{Br}^-$ to give $\text{RCOOH} + \text{HBr}$ (as products).
